column1: In classical yoga philosophy, what was the original purpose of asana (physical postures)?
column2: To serve as physical scaffolding stabilizing the body sufficiently to endure prolonged seated meditation and breath control without biomechanical distraction or tissue failure.

column1: In Samkhya philosophy, what are Purusha and Prakriti, and how does this map to exercise science?
column2: Purusha is pure consciousness (the observer); Prakriti is matter/physiology. In exercise terms, this maps to the separation between the observing mind and the physiological substrate being trained (interoception vs. autonomic stillness).

column1: What are the three Gunas and their physiological analogs?
column2: Tamas = inertia/degenerative stagnation (parasympathetic lethargy); Rajas = activity/kinetic energy (sympathetic drive, motor unit recruitment); Sattva = harmony/equilibrium (parasympathetic dominance, high vagal tone, optimal HRV, low cortisol).

column1: What is the foundational invariant of all asana practice regarding joints and muscular effort?
column2: Joint centration precedes muscular effort — articular surfaces must be optimally congruent with balanced capsular tension before force generation, or load will concentrate at a focal point rather than disperse evenly.

column1: What happens biomechanically when a hip joint is loaded in internal rotation with an adducted femur (e.g., in Warrior I with limited thoracic rotation)?
column2: Force is directed toward the anterior-superior labrum, a fibrocartilage region with limited vascular supply and limited healing capacity, instead of distributing evenly across the femoral head and acetabular cartilage.

column1: List the three governing mechanical invariants of asana practice described in Lesson 2.
column2: 1) Proximal stability enables distal mobility. 2) Force couples must balance (agonist torque counterbalanced by antagonist/stabilizer). 3) The kinetic chain is continuous — compensation at one joint propagates to others unless intercepted.

column1: What is the primary chemical driver of respiration in a healthy person, and what is the common misconception?
column2: Primary driver is arterial CO₂ tension (PaCO₂), sensed by central (medulla) and peripheral (carotid/aortic body) chemoreceptors — not oxygen demand. PaO₂ only drives respiration when it drops below ~60 mmHg.

column1: What physiological shifts occur with hyperventilation vs. hypoventilation/breath retention (kumbhaka) in pranayama?
column2: Hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂ (hypocapnia), causing respiratory alkalosis (pH rises). Hypoventilation/kumbhaka raises PaCO₂ (hypercapnia), causing respiratory acidosis (pH falls).

column1: What is Respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia (RSA) and what breathing rate maximizes its resonance effect?
column2: RSA is the natural oscillation of heart rate with breathing (HR rises on inhale, falls on exhale) via vagal tone modulation. Slow breathing at ~0.1 Hz (~6 breaths/min) resonates with baroreceptor-mediated blood pressure oscillations, maximizing HRV coupling.

column1: What is the fundamental invariant governing yoga's adaptive mechanism compared to resistance training?
column2: Yoga applies progressive overload to passive tissue extensibility (time-under-tension via bodyweight/gravity, triggering fibroblast proliferation and collagen realignment) rather than to contractile force production as in resistance training.

column1: How does sustained isometric holding at end-range in yoga affect the stretch reflex mechanism?
column2: It desensitizes Golgi tendon organs and recalibrates gamma motor neuron firing thresholds, attenuating the protective stretch reflex and allowing greater passive range of motion over time.

column1: Name three structural/metabolic sources of individual variation in yoga flexibility gains.
column2: 1) Collagen fiber composition (Type I vs. Type III ratio) affecting rate and durability of ROM gains. 2) Bony anatomy (limb length, acetabular depth, femoral version) creating hard mechanical limits. 3) Fascial hydration and myofascial sliding capacity, affected by inflammation, hydration, and prior injury/adhesions.
